t.4.29.1: When Sugrīva had entered his cave and the sky had been freed of clouds, Rāma, who had dwelt there through the nights of the rainy season, was sorely afflicted by longing and grief.
t.4.29.2: Seeing the pale sky and the spotless orb of the moon, and seeing too the autumn night anointed with moonlight,
t.4.29.3: Realizing that Sugrīva was given over to pleasure, that Janaka's daughter was lost, and that the appointed time had passed, he grew bewildered, deeply distressed.
t.4.29.4: But the wise Rāghava, regaining consciousness after a moment, once again thought of Vaidehī, though she already dwelt in his mind.
t.4.29.5: Seated on the summit of the mountain, which was adorned with golden minerals, he beheld the autumn sky and went in his mind to his beloved.
t.4.29.6: And seeing the spotless sky, from which the lightning and the clouds had departed and which resounded with the cries of cranes, he lamented in an anguished voice.
t.4.29.7: That young woman of mine, whose voice was like the cry of the sārasa cranes, and who delighted in the hermitage amid the resounding calls of the sārasas, how can she find delight today?
t.4.29.8: Having seen the flowering asana trees, spotless as if made of gold, how can that young woman take any delight, seeing them yet not seeing me?
t.4.29.9: She who once used to wake to the cry of the kalahaṃsas, sweet-voiced and lovely in every limb, how does she, my beloved, wake today?
t.4.29.10: Hearing the cries of the cakravāka birds that roam together with their mates, how will she fare, she whose eyes are large as lotuses?
t.4.29.11: Wandering among lakes, rivers, ponds, groves and forests without her, the fawn-eyed one, I find no happiness today.
t.4.29.13: Thus and in like words the king's son, best of men, lamented, as the sāraṅga bird cries out for water from the lord of the thirty gods.
t.4.29.14: Then the glorious Lakṣmaṇa, having roamed about the lovely mountain slopes in search of fruit, returned and saw his elder brother.
t.4.29.12: I hope that longing, made unremitting by the charms of autumn, does not torment too severely that lovely lady, because of her separation from me and her delicate tenderness.
t.4.29.15: Seeing him alone in that lonely place, overwhelmed by unbearable brooding and almost senseless, the high-minded Saumitri, himself wretched with anguish because of his brother's despondency, spoke to Rāma.
t.4.29.16: Noble one, what is the use of falling under the sway of desire, and what is the use of the defeat of your own manly strength? This resolve is forever being abandoned; what is gained here by turning away from the effort?
t.4.29.17: O you of undaunted spirit, make these the basis of your success: diligent application to action, serenity of mind, timing guided by focused deliberation, the strength of your allies, and the cause that underlies your own undertaking.
t.4.29.18: O lord of the race of Manu, Jānakī, who has you as her protector, is not easily won by another; for no one who approaches a blazing crest of fire escapes being burned, O worthy one, foremost among heroes.
t.4.29.19: Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who bore auspicious marks and was unassailable, words that came from his own nature: beneficial and wholesome, grounded in sound policy, conciliatory, and in harmony with dharma and artha.
t.4.29.20: The task must be attended to without doubt, for the proper course of action must indeed be followed. Surely, once the prince's formidable undertaking has been set in motion, its reward ought not to be weighed.
t.4.29.21: Then Rāma, thinking of Maithilī, whose eyes were like lotus petals, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with a face that was withering away.
t.4.29.22: Having satisfied the earth with water and brought the crops to fruition, the thousand-eyed one, his work accomplished, now rests.
t.4.29.23: O son of a king, the clouds, with their smooth and deep rumbling, moving at the head of the mountains and trees, have poured out their water and are now exhausted.
t.4.29.24: Dark as the petals of the blue lotus, the clouds, having darkened the ten directions, now have their force spent, like elephants whose rut has passed.
t.4.29.25: O gentle one, the rain-bearing winds that had risen up, laden with water, of great force and fragrant with kuṭaja and arjuna blossoms, have roamed about and now subsided.
t.4.29.27: Rained upon by great clouds, the mountains with their variegated peaks, washed clean and spotless, shine as though anointed with the rays of the moon.
t.4.29.26: O Lakṣmaṇa, O sinless one, the roar of the clouds, of the elephants, of the peacocks and of the cascading streams has suddenly fallen silent.
t.4.29.28: The autumn rivers slowly, slowly reveal their sandbanks, as young women, bashful at their first union, slowly reveal their hips.
t.4.29.29: O gentle one, the lakes shine forth with their clear waters, resounding with the cries of ospreys and thronged with flocks of cakravāka birds.
t.4.29.30: O son of a king, O gentle one, the time has come for kings who bear enmity toward one another and are eager for conquest to set out on their campaigns.
t.4.29.31: This is that first season for the marching forth of kings, O son of a king, yet I see neither Sugrīva nor any such preparation.
t.4.29.32: O gentle one, the four months of the rainy season have passed like a hundred years for me, tormented by grief and unable to see Sītā.
t.4.29.33: O Lakṣmaṇa, King Sugrīva shows no compassion toward me, though I am parted from my beloved, stricken with sorrow, robbed of my kingdom and driven into exile.
t.4.29.34: He is helpless, robbed of his kingdom and assaulted by Rāvaṇa; wretched, far from home and lovesick, he has come to me alone for refuge.
t.4.29.35: For these reasons, gentle one, O scorcher of foes, I have been slighted by the evil-minded Sugrīva, king of the monkeys.
t.4.29.37: Enter Kiṣkindhā and, on my word, speak to Sugrīva, that bull among the monkeys, the fool who is attached to vulgar pleasures.
t.4.29.38: He who, having made a promise, destroys the hope of petitioners who have come to him, and of those who once did him a favour, is the lowest of men in the world.
t.4.29.36: Having fixed the time for the search for Sītā and made the agreement, that evil-minded one, now that his own purpose is achieved, does not take notice of it.
t.4.29.39: Whether it be good or evil, he who holds fast with truth to the word he has spoken is a hero, the best among men.
t.4.29.41: Surely they wish to behold the form of my gold-backed bow, drawn by me in battle, gleaming like a mass of lightning flashes.
t.4.29.40: Those who, once their own aims are fulfilled, do not stand by friends whose aims remain unfulfilled are ingrates, and such ingrates not even flesh-eating creatures will feed upon, though they lie dead.
t.4.29.42: He wishes to hear once more the terrible twang of my bowstring against my palm, like the crash of a thunderbolt, when I am enraged in battle.
t.4.29.43: Indeed, even though things have come to this pass and his prowess is fully known, I, who have you as my ally, O hero, O son of a king, would have no anxiety.
t.4.29.44: O conqueror of enemy cities, the lord of the monkeys, now that his own purpose is achieved, no longer acknowledges the agreement for whose sake this undertaking was made.
t.4.29.45: Though the lord of the monkeys had made a promise fixing the time as the end of the rainy season, he, absorbed in his pleasures, does not perceive that the four months have passed.
t.4.29.46: Sporting with his council of ministers, he gives himself over only to drinking; Sugrīva shows no compassion to us, who are wretched with grief.
t.4.29.47: Go, dear one of great strength, and let Sugrīva be told by you what the form of my anger is; and you should speak these words to him.
t.4.29.49: Vālī alone was slain by me in battle with a single arrow; but you, who have strayed from the truth, I shall slay together with your kinsmen.
t.4.29.48: The path by which the slain Vālī went has not grown narrow. Stand by the agreement, Sugrīva, and do not follow the path of Vālī.
t.4.29.50: Therefore, now that the task has been so arranged, O bull among men, tell whatever is beneficial, O best of men; make haste, for the appointed time is passing.
t.4.29.51: O lord of the monkeys, keep your word to me, mindful of the eternal dharma you pledged, lest today, struck down by the arrows I let fly, you die and go to the abode of Yama and there behold Vālin.
t.4.29.52: Seeing his elder brother, whose anger had grown intense, lamenting again and again in distress, he of fierce splendour, the lord of the human dynasty, formed a harsh resolve against the lord of the monkeys.
